replacement: “To Grushenka, then!” Alyosha exclaimed sadly, clasping his hands. “Can Rakitin really have told the truth? I thought you’d only called on her, and that was all.”
“Mitya, you are unhappy, yes! But not as unhappy as you think. Don’t torment yourself to death with despair.”

“I know he won’t. I know it perfectly well, and now more than ever. And that’s not all. I know something else. Only a few days ago, perhaps just yesterday, he understood for the first time _in earnest_ (underline _in earnest_) that Grushenka may not be joking after all, and really means to marry me. He knows what she’s like; he knows the cat. So do you imagine he’ll give me money to help that along, when he’s mad about her himself? And that isn’t all, either. I can tell you more than that. I know that for the past five days he’s had three thousand drawn from the bank, changed into notes of a hundred roubles, packed into a big envelope, sealed with five seals and tied crosswise with red tape. You see how well informed I am! On the envelope he’s written: ‘To my angel Grushenka, when she will come to me.’ He scrawled it himself, silently and in secret, and nobody knows the money is there except the valet Smerdyakov, whom he trusts as he trusts himself. So for three or four days now he’s been expecting Grushenka. He hopes she’ll come for the money. He’s sent word to her about it, and she’s sent word back that perhaps she’ll come. And if she does go to the old man, can I marry her afterwards? Now you see why I’m here in secret, and what I’m keeping watch for.”
